findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating ongoing organisational capacity strain, with score increased this quarter
findings.detail: CR 041 (amber, score increased from 8 to 12 this quarter due to impact increase from marginal to moderate) identifies that 'Capacity issues generated by Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)' are a material risk. The register notes that 'work will not be able to be progressed with sufficient speed to meet the tight timescales and may impact on the delivery of other work'. The Mayoral election has been postponed from May 2026 to May 2028, and Norfolk is consolidating to three new unitaries by April 2028, with partnerships and workstreams now in place across all eight existing authorities.
findings.matters: A lender should track whether LGR is stretching management's capacity to deliver core services and financial management. The delay in the Mayoral election and two-year transition period adds uncertainty to council structure and resources.
findings.figures: Score increased from 8 to 12 this quarter; Mayoral election postponed to May 2028; consolidation to three new unitaries by April 2028
findings.quote: Capacity issues generated by Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)

findings.headline: Housing delivery target increased by 70% (from 557 to 932 homes per annum) but current performance is only 87% of previous lower target
findings.detail: CR 010 (green rating, but concerning trajectory) records that the revised government framework set the housing requirement at 932 new homes per annum, a 70% increase. However, the most recent Housing Delivery Test showed delivery averaged 87% of the old (lower) target. The register forecasts this 'is forecast to fall because of persistent under delivery over the previous three-year period' and recommends 'a 20% buffer will need to be added to the housing requirement moving forwards, unless completion rates (and planning permission rates) increase'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand housing trajectory risk. Persistent underdelivery against a much higher target suggests planning constraints, developer confidence, or market conditions that could impact future council tax base growth and developer contribution income.
findings.figures: Housing delivery target increased to 932 per annum (from 557); current delivery averaging 87% of previous target; 20% buffer now needed
findings.quote: The revised nation government framework (dec 2024) increases the target further to 932 new homes per annum (approximately 70% increase)

findings.headline: Uncertainty over the 27/28 budget position due to awaiting service costs and Local Government Reorganisation implications
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Plan remains a red-rated risk with residual score 16. Although 2025/26 closed with a £354k underspend and 2026/27 has a balanced budget, the register explicitly flags that uncertainty exists for 27/28 'due to awaiting service costs from external providers and the Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) position'. Budget monitoring at period 4 is due to forecast the outturn based on latest information.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council will face a structural deficit in 27/28 and whether the 2026/27 balance is sustainable or dependent on timing of known costs.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates significant governance, financial and capacity implications through 2028 transition period.
findings.detail: North Norfolk will form part of a new East Norfolk Unitary Council alongside Great Yarmouth and parts of South Norfolk and Broadland, effective 1 April 2028. Shadow elections and arrangements are expected May 2027. The council acknowledges this creates significant governance, financial, operational and capacity implications during the transition period while maintaining business-as-usual service delivery. The August 2026 Progress Tracker notes that pressures from LGR have caused delays in completing Service Plans.
findings.matters: Major local government restructure creates uncertainty over governance continuity, leadership stability, and resource availability during a critical period. Concurrent transition demands and policy backlogs compound the risk of control slippage.
findings.figures: Reorganisation effective 1 April 2028; shadow elections May 2027; Progress Tracker notes LGR delays to budget and planning work
findings.quote: On 25 March 2026, the Secretary of State announced the Government's decision to proceed, subject to Parliamentary approval, with the establishment of three unitary councils for Norfolk.

findings.headline: Policy and strategy documents overdue for review due to capacity constraints and staff gaps, risking misalignment with priorities.
findings.detail: The council has identified that several policy and strategy documents are overdue for review and update. The stated reason is capacity issues and lack of appropriate staff in post to undertake reviews. This creates risk that policies do not reflect current corporate priorities or best practice. Examples include the Risk Management Policy and Partnership Framework.
findings.matters: Outdated policies and strategies create control gaps and may result in decisions made against obsolete guidance. When capacity constraints prevent policy updates, it signals resource stress that affects governance maturity.
findings.figures: Policy reviews delayed; target completion 31 December 2026 for Policy and Strategy updates; Partnership Framework review also overdue
findings.quote: Several of the Council's policy and strategy documents are overdue for review and updating and there is a risk that these documents do not reflect current corporate priorities and best practice if the reviews are delayed. The delay in updating policies is mainly driven by capacity issues and having the appropriate staff in post to undertake the reviews.

findings.headline: Service Plans and team budgets are not aligned, with managers reporting uncertain resource targeting and risk of misallocation.
findings.detail: Multiple managers reported that Service Plans and Team Plans have not been updated and that budgets may not be aligned with planned service delivery. This creates risk that resources are not targeted efficiently and that under-resourced areas may not meet performance targets. Action plan target for resolution is December 2026, but this was also identified in the prior year progress tracker and remains in progress.
findings.matters: Unaligned budgets and service plans suggest resource allocation decisions lack visibility or control, increasing risk of overspend in unfunded areas or underspend in priority services.
findings.figures: Completion target 31 December 2026; flagged in both prior and current year action plans
findings.quote: Several managers referred to the need for further development of the Service and Team Plans to help ensure that resources are targeted in the most efficient way and to ensure that budgets are aligned with service delivery.

findings.headline: Project Management Framework in place for over two years but not adopted universally across the council, representing a governance weakness.
findings.detail: The council has a Project Management Framework to ensure consistent governance of projects. However, the framework is acknowledged not to be used universally despite being in place for over two years. The council states it will enforce use across the whole organisation, but this work remains outstanding.
findings.matters: Inconsistent use of project governance frameworks creates risk that capital and strategic projects lack proper oversight, approval controls and budgetary discipline—areas critical to financial stability.
findings.figures: Project Management Framework in place over 2 years, not universally adopted
findings.quote: Whilst this has been in place for over two years the framework is not being adopted universally across the council and so at present this does represent a weakness in governance.

findings.headline: Backlog of 23 overdue audit recommendations, including recommendations from 2021/22, showing slow implementation.
findings.detail: Outstanding audit recommendations increased from 19 (2024/25) to 23 (2025/26). Of these, one relates to an audit in 2021/22, five to 2024/25 audits, and twelve to 2025/26. The council has initiated monthly CLT review of recommendations but significant delays remain, including recommendations more than 3 years old.
findings.matters: A growing backlog of overdue audit recommendations suggests management is not prioritising control improvements, and the age of some recommendations (since 2021) indicates systemic implementation weakness that poses ongoing control risk.
findings.figures: 23 audit recommendations outstanding (19 in prior year); 1 from 2021/22, 5 from 2024/25, 12 from 2025/26; only 1 currently overdue from 2021/22 cohort
findings.quote: There were 23 audit recommendation outstanding at the year-end 2025/26 (19 outstanding as at year ending 2024/25).

findings.headline: Four years of accounts issued with disclaimed audit opinions, a significant break in audit assurance.
findings.detail: The 2021–22 to 2024-25 Statements of Accounts were issued with disclaimed audit opinions. This reflects sustained challenges in the local government audit market including auditor capacity issues. The council submitted accounts ahead of backstop dates, but the lack of audit opinion on accounts for four consecutive years is a material control indicator.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions mean auditors could not form any opinion on whether accounts are fairly stated. For a lender, this is the baseline assurance that accounts are reliable—without it, the council's financial position cannot be verified.
findings.figures: 2021–22 to 2024-25 Statements of Accounts issued with disclaimed audit opinions

findings.matters: This represents a structural demand-driven cost pressure that the council cannot fully pass through and must absorb from reserves. If homelessness continues to rise, this cost pressure will persist and compound, eroding the council's buffer.

findings.detail: The council budgeted £279k to finance capital from revenue but is now forecasting £1.35 million. This £1.07 million swing indicates capital projects are either costing more than expected or proceeding faster than planned, consuming more of available revenue resources.
findings.matters: Additional capital financing from revenue reduces the council's financial headroom and signals either a capital programme in trouble or financing assumptions that have proven wrong.
findings.figures: Budgeted £278.6k, forecast £1.354m, variance £1.075m
findings.quote: Revenue Financing for Capital: 278,600 278,600 1,353,540 1,074,940

findings.paper_title: Appx A General Fund Summary Budget Monitoring P4 2026-27
findings.headline: Resources department is forecasting £1.3 million overspend, the largest variance across all services
findings.detail: Resources is now forecasting £8.6 million spend against a base budget of £7.3 million—an 18% overspend. This is by far the largest departmental issue. The overspend is already evident at P4 (four months in), suggesting persistent cost pressures rather than timing variance.
findings.matters: A material departmental overspend this early in the year signals either loss of budget control or substantive service cost increases; both are concerning to a lender assessing the council's financial management capability.
findings.figures: Resources budgeted £7.3m, forecast £8.6m, variance £1.296m

findings.headline: Legal Services is simultaneously operating with vacant permanent posts and incurring substantial agency staffing costs
findings.detail: Legal Services shows £58,715 in underspend from vacant permanent posts, but simultaneously reports £49,140 in agency staff costs in the supplies budget. The offsetting positions suggest the department is meeting staffing needs through agency cover rather than permanent recruitment.
findings.matters: Sustained agency spend paired with vacancies may indicate recruitment difficulties or persistent service demands that the permanent structure is not meeting, affecting staffing cost predictability and service continuity.
findings.figures: £58,715 (vacant post savings), £49,140 (agency staff)
findings.quote: £49,140 Agency staff. (£6,000) Disbursement fees.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation staffing cost is being funded from reserves
findings.detail: Human Resources & Payroll shows a £26,086 overspend in the forecast outturn due to an LGR post that is being funded from reserves. This represents a drawdown of reserves to cover an operating cost related to the reorganisation.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns for operating costs reduce the council's financial resilience; lenders monitor reserve levels as a key indicator of capacity to absorb unexpected shocks or funding gaps.
findings.quote: LGR post funded from reserves.

findings.headline: Benefits Subsidy and Business Rates outturn remain provisional and subject to external audit change
findings.detail: The report notes that Benefits Subsidy and Business Rates Retention figures incorporated into the outturn are provisional and will be subject to external audit later in the year. A DWP audit could result in repayment demands. The council holds earmarked reserves to mitigate such risks, but the outcome is not yet known.
findings.matters: Material financial figures classified as provisional indicate that the final outturn could differ; a lender needs to know this position is not final
findings.figures: Benefits Subsidy return submitted 05 May 2026, subject to audit; NNDR3 return submitted 22 May 2025, subject to audit
findings.quote: Depending on the outcome from the external audit review there could be an impact on the overall financial position, for example should a subsidy repayment be due to the Department for Work and Pensions. It is for this reason that the Council holds a Benefits Earmarked Reserve to mitigate any such impact.

findings.headline: Business rates calculation remains uncertain since 2020/21; exit from pooling arrangement suggests reduced pooling benefit
findings.detail: The council has held all business rates surpluses in reserve since 2020/21 due to ongoing difficulty calculating its retained business rates share and risk of having to repay central government. For 2026/27, the council exited the Norfolk Business Rates Pool due to rule changes making the scheme "less attractive." This signals volatility in a material income source.
findings.matters: Business rates are a major local income stream; uncertainty in calculation and exit from pooling suggest forecast volatility and reduced access to pooling stabilisation
findings.figures: Surpluses retained since 2020/21 in Business Rates Reserve; pooling exited for 2026/27
findings.quote: Since 2020/21 it has been difficult to calculate the budget for the Council's Retained Business Rates because of this. Changes to the business rates pooling rules, making the scheme less attractive, influenced the decision for Norfolk authorities to not enter a pooling arrangement for 2026/27.

findings.headline: £5m PWLB loan taken to cover cash flow deficit that has persisted since March 2023
findings.detail: The council took a £5m Public Works Loan Board loan in 2025/26 to address a cash flow shortfall identified 18 months earlier. The report states the loan was taken temporarily "as interest rates remained higher" and "If the loan is no longer needed in 2026/27 it will not be renewed." This framing suggests the deficit may be structural rather than temporary.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's cash position is sustainably positive or whether external borrowing masks operating cash constraints
findings.figures: £5m PWLB loan; cash flow deficit identified March 2023
findings.quote: Since March 2023 it was identified that the Council had a cashflow deficit of £5m. A PWLB loan was taken for 1 year in 2025/26 as interest rates remained higher, although decreasing. If the loan is no longer needed in 2026/27 it will not be renewed.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast to fall £0.517m short of approved project commitments in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has only £1.882m of capital receipts available but £2.399m of capital projects already approved requiring receipts funding. The report flags this as "forecasted to be an issue" and advises that new capital projects will need to be funded by borrowing instead. The shortfall depends on uncertain inflows from Right to Buy income and Disabled Facilities Grant repayments.
findings.matters: A funding gap forcing reliance on borrowing for discretionary projects signals either declining property sales income or overcommitment of receipts; both affect financial flexibility
findings.figures: £1.882m receipts available vs £2.399m committed = potential £0.517m shortfall
findings.quote: However, the Council only has £1.882m of capital receipts funding available as at the end of 2025/26 (potential shortfall of £0.517m). This is forecasted to be an issue

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 34% of planned spending; £25m budget underspend driven by project delays
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £13.170m against an updated budget of £38.280m, leaving £25.111m unspent (66%). The report attributes this to high-value projects not progressing as planned and timelines being reconsidered. Large property acquisitions (non-housing) accounted for much of the slippage. This pattern suggests forecasting difficulty or project delivery risk.
findings.matters: Repeated capital underspend raises questions about the council's ability to deliver planned infrastructure and whether budget forecasts are realistic
findings.figures: £13.170m actual expenditure vs £38.280m updated budget = £25.111m underspend (66%)
findings.quote: This underspend is attributable to multiple factors. Some high value projects have not progressed as far as originally planned due to project delays, or project timelines have been reconsidered to reflect changes to programmed delivery.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs exceed recoverable subsidy by £0.611m
findings.detail: The council's spending on temporary accommodation (bed and breakfast for nightly homelessness) exceeds what can be recovered through the housing benefit subsidy scheme because expenditure is capped. The £0.611m shortfall was offset by releasing £0.400m from the Council Tax second homes premium reserve. This is not a one-off adjustment but reflects structural pressure in homelessness provision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can sustain rising homelessness costs; relying on one-off reserves to cover recurring service deficits signals unsustainable pressures
findings.figures: £0.611m subsidy shortfall; £0.400m transferred from Council Tax second homes premium reserve
findings.quote: This shortfall is largely in respect of temporary accommodation costs which the council pays in respect of nightly homelessness provision (Bed and Breakfast charges) due to the capping of expenditure level we cannot recover all the expense through subsidy.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: The auditors have identified a formal Value for Money significant weakness in governance arrangements relating to audit support and statutory reporting compliance.
findings.detail: This is a documented VFM risk that will be reported in the Auditor's Annual Report. The auditors assess that 'significant improvements are required in the Council's arrangements to support the rebuilding of assurance' and assess 'whether the pre-2023/24 gaps in assurance can be sufficiently addressed.'
findings.matters: A formal documented significant weakness in governance arrangements is a regulatory flag that directly impacts credit assessment and would influence lending decisions.
findings.figures: Governance VFM risk identified for 2025/26; areas for improvement identified across timeliness, quality, and delivery of financial reporting
findings.quote: We have identified a value for money risk of significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to effectively support an audit of its financial statements and the Council's ability to publish their unaudited accounts by the statutory deadline.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: Right of Use Assets including £10.1 million in peppercorn leases lack supporting valuation evidence, preventing audit assurance.
findings.detail: The auditors were unable to obtain assurance over Right of Use Asset valuations for 2024/25 and specifically note that 'there was no supporting valuation evidence provided by the client for the ROU valuation of Peppercorn Leases.' This represents a significant balance sheet item without evidenced valuation.
findings.matters: Lack of supporting valuation evidence for a £10.1 million balance sheet item prevents credible financial reporting and suggests potential misstatement of asset values.
findings.figures: £10.1 million peppercorn lease ROU assets in prior year balance sheet; Right of Use Asset total was £10.308 million
findings.quote: We were unable to obtain assurance over valuation of Right of Use Assets (ROU) 24/25 and there was no supporting valuation evidence provided by the client for the ROU valuation of Peppercorn Leases. The peppercorn lease ROU assets were £10.1 million in the prior year.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: The auditors cannot obtain full assurance over reserve balances and do not expect to rebuild assurance over historic positions during 2025/26.
findings.detail: Auditors anticipate 'limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26' and 'limited assurance over the closing PPE and closing reserves balance, due to uncertainty over the opening amount.' They state it is 'unlikely that we will commence any rebuilding of assurance over the historic position during the 2025/26 audit cycle.'
findings.matters: Inability to assure reserve balances prevents the council from credibly demonstrating its financial position and sustainability, a critical factor for credit assessment.
findings.figures: £10.1 million in peppercorn lease Right of Use Assets in prior year with no supporting valuation evidence provided
findings.quote: Limited assurance over the closing PPE and closing reserves balance, due to uncertainty over the opening amount... it is unlikely that we will commence any rebuilding of assurance over the historic position during the 2025/26 audit cycle.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: A large number of material misstatements were identified in 2024/25 financial statements and required correction by management.
findings.detail: Misstatements included: unsupported PPE impairments, incorrect period recognition of capital additions, inappropriate capitalisation, delayed asset reclassifications, incorrect classifications of assets held for sale, and incorrect valuation methodologies. These were rated as 'Ineffective' in the council's controls.
findings.matters: The volume and nature of material errors corrected by auditors indicates the internal control environment is not operating effectively, raising concerns about the reliability of financial data and management oversight.
findings.figures: Multiple material misstatements across PPE (£94.695m balance), cash and investments (£1.784m and £0.638m variances), and other balance sheet areas
findings.quote: A large number of material misstatements were detected as a result of our work which was corrected by management.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: The section 151 Officer departed after the 2023/24 audit and the Collection Fund officer also left during the period, creating capacity gaps during financial statement rebuild.
findings.detail: The council's section 151 Officer left just after the 2023/24 audit finished, with a replacement only joining just before the 2024/25 year-end audit commenced. The officer responsible for the Collection Fund also departed. These departures contributed to audit delays and material misstatements.
findings.matters: Loss of experienced finance leadership during a critical rebuild phase creates ongoing risk of control failures and financial reporting errors, particularly where institutional knowledge is required.
findings.figures: Two senior finance positions affected during audit period
findings.quote: The Council's section 151 Officer left the Council just after the 2023/24 audit finished. The Council engaged a new section 151 Officer just before the year-end audit was due to start. The officer responsible for the Collection Fund also left the Council.

findings.paper_title: North Norfolk DC Provisional Audit Planning Report 25-26
findings.headline: North Norfolk has received disclaimer opinions on three consecutive years of accounts and failed to publish accounts by the statutory deadline for four consecutive years.
findings.detail: The council received disclaimer opinions for 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24 financial statements. The 2024/25 accounts were only published on 18 July 2025, missing the 30 June 2025 statutory deadline under the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015.
findings.matters: Serial audit failures and missed publication deadlines indicate fundamental control weaknesses affecting the council's financial reporting credibility and ability to demonstrate its financial position to potential lenders.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years unable to meet publication deadlines (2021/22 through 2024/25); three consecutive years of disclaimer opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24)
findings.quote: The Council had been unable to publish its statement of accounts for the years 2021/2022, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 by the target dates required by the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: £5m PWLB loan matures 1 May 2026 and must refinance at rates 45-113 basis points higher than current
findings.detail: The council's £5m PWLB loan set at 4.59% matures on 1 May 2026 (seven weeks after the statement date). At 31 March 2026, prevailing PWLB rates were substantially higher: 1-year at 5.04%, 5-year at 5.28%, 10-year at 5.72%. The council faces forced refinancing at materially higher cost. Locking in longer duration to avoid repeated refinancing risk would increase the burden further.
findings.matters: Refinancing at higher rates increases annual borrowing costs. Rolling over at the current 1-year rate (5.04% vs 4.59% existing) adds approximately £22,500 to annual interest expense. Opting for longer-dated borrowing to reduce refinancing risk would increase costs further, creating material budget pressure.
findings.figures: Current loan rate 4.59%, current 1-year PWLB rate 5.04% (45bps higher), 5-year 5.28% (69bps higher), 10-year 5.72% (113bps higher)
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council renewed a £5m long-term loan with the PWLB (Central Government Public Works Loans Board) running from the 1st of May 2025 to 1st of May 2026, secured at an interest rate of 4.59%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 34% of budget, signalling significant delivery failure
findings.detail: The council budgeted £38.280m in capital expenditure for 2025/26 but only delivered £13.112m, a 66% shortfall of £25.2m. Unfinanced capital expenditure (the actual borrowing requirement) was £0.587m against a budget of £5.613m, confirming that planned capital projects were not executed. This represents a marked deterioration from 2024/25 when actual spend (£25.702m) was close to budget.
findings.matters: Substantial capital underspend indicates project delays, cancellations, or management problems that impact infrastructure delivery and raise concerns about capital strategy execution and borrowing forecasting accuracy.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure budget £38.280m actual £13.112m (£25.2m shortfall, 66%); unfinanced capital budget £5.613m actual £0.587m (£5.0m shortfall, 89%)
findings.quote: Capital expenditure 25.702 38.280 13.112

findings.headline: Council forecasts £2.03 million budget gap over three years; prior-year savings delivery fell short of target
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a significant budget gap of £2.03 million from 2025/26 to 2028/29, driven by inflationary pressures, funding cuts, demographic changes, and uncertainty around future government funding reforms. The council has proposed a comprehensive savings plan totalling £8.23 million across this period, which if fully achieved would leave a net projected surplus of £6.21 million. However, delivery risk is evident: in 2024/25, the council achieved only 64% of its planned savings target, delivering £0.62 million against a £0.97 million target.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether the council's substantial savings plans are realistic and achievable. The shortfall in prior-year savings delivery (64%) raises questions about the council's ability to realise the larger planned savings and maintain financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £2.03 million budget gap (2025/26–2028/29), £8.23 million planned savings, £6.21 million net projected surplus, £0.62m achieved vs £0.97m target in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council delivered £0.62 million savings , 64% of planned savings for 2024/25

findings.headline: Governance weakness identified: council unable to publish accounts by statutory deadline following key finance staff departures
findings.detail: The auditor identified a significant weakness in the council's governance arrangements—specifically its ability to effectively support an audit of financial statements and publish unaudited accounts by the statutory deadline. The 2024/25 accounts were not published until 18 July 2025, 18 days late. This continues a pattern from prior years (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24). The Section 151 Officer left the council just after the 2023/24 audit finished, and a replacement was engaged only just before the 2024/25 year-end audit started. The officer responsible for the Collection Fund also left. Working papers did not consistently meet quality standards or agreed delivery timetables, contributing to incomplete audit procedures.
findings.matters: Inability to produce timely, accurate accounts indicates weak financial governance and insufficient resource capacity. For a lender, this signals the council may struggle with other financial reporting obligations, statutory compliance, and effective financial controls during a critical period.
findings.figures: 18 July 2025 publication (vs 30 June deadline), Section 151 Officer turnover during 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council's section 151 Officer left the Council just after the 2023/24 audit finished. The Council engaged a new section 151 Officer just before the year-end audit was due to start. The officer responsible for the Collection Fund also left the Council.

findings.headline: Auditors unable to issue audit opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to insufficient evidence; significant weaknesses in accounting controls
findings.detail: The external auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements on 17 February 2026, meaning they were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide reasonable assurance over in-year movements, closing balances, and prior-year comparatives. The council's draft accounts contained a large number of material misstatements that required correction by management. The auditor cannot obtain assurance over opening balances from prior years or many specific account balances including property/plant/equipment valuations and reserves. This continues from prior years (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 all had similar issues), and the auditor projects the council will likely require another disclaimer in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on published financial statements to understand the council's true financial position or creditworthiness. A disclaimer of opinion indicates fundamental failures in the council's accounting infrastructure and governance.
findings.figures: 17 February 2026 (disclaimer date), 2021/22–2024/25 (continuous disclaimer history)
findings.quote: we were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances

findings.headline: Procurement strategy outdated and not updated for Procurement Act 2023 requirements
findings.detail: Current Procurement Strategy implemented October 2021 with a review date of May 2025. Strategy does not reflect Procurement Act 2023 requirements. Only one Procurement Officer in post; limited training has been provided to other staff on PA2023, and the council accepts the risk of non-compliant procurement outside the officer's control.
findings.matters: An outdated strategy increases the risk of non-compliant procurement decisions, legal challenges, and weak contract management. Staff unaware of PA2023 may conduct procurements that fail to meet statutory requirements or offer poor value.
findings.figures: Strategy review due May 2025, now overdue; single Procurement Officer resource
findings.quote: The current Procurement Strategy was implemented as of October 2021 with a listed review date of May 2025, indicating that the current strategy is outdated and requires review. As a result, the current strategy does not reflect the requirements of PA2023.

findings.headline: Section 106 developer contributions management fragmented, with unspent funds exceeding spend deadlines
findings.detail: One urgent recommendation flagged unspent available amounts that have exceeded their 'spend deadline' dates. New S106 officer recruited January 2026 on 0.8 FTE. Multiple important recommendations on tracking obligations, recording developer progress, and accuracy of publicly available records on Exacom. Old agreements (pre-2012) still have complex unallocated spend.
findings.matters: Section 106 is legally binding money owed to the council for services or held on account for future work. Unspent sums past deadline risk repayment to developers or audit failure. Poor tracking suggests capital and obligations are not being actively managed.
findings.figures: Available amounts exceeded spend deadlines; one urgent recommendation issued
findings.quote: To review all unspent available amounts that have exceeded their 'spend deadline' dates and take appropriate action in accordance with the s106 agreements.

findings.headline: Bank and creditor reconciliations repeatedly delayed beyond the one-month control standard
findings.detail: November 2025 creditor reconciliation was not completed until 20 January 2026 (nearly 2 months late). July 2025 bank reconciliation delayed to 9 October 2025 (over 2 months). Multiple other instances of reconciliations prepared and reviewed 2–3 months after period end, rather than within one month as required.
findings.matters: Timely reconciliation is a basic financial control; delays hide errors and create audit risk. Systematic delay suggests understaffing, process failure, or prioritization below acceptable standards.
findings.figures: November 2025 reconciliation completed 20 January 2026; July 2025 reconciliation completed 9 October 2025
findings.quote: The July 2025 Receipts Account reconciliation was not performed by the Senior Finance Officer until 9th October 2025 and was reviewed on 10th October 2025.

findings.headline: Debt write-off approved above the authorizer's documented limit
findings.detail: A write-off over £5k was authorized by the Chief Group Accountant, who believed their limit was £10k. The Authorised Signatories List states it as £5k. The authorization breached the formal limit and the discrepancy shows the list and delegation are out of sync.
findings.matters: Authorization limits exist to prevent large decisions going to junior officers. A breached limit signals that financial delegation is not controlled or monitored.
findings.figures: One write-off exceeding £5k
findings.quote: One debt write-off in excess of £5k was incorrectly authorised by the Chief Group Accountant. It was believed that the Chief Group Accountant could authorise write-offs up to £10k but this was not formally reflected in the Authorised Signatories List where the limit is recorded as £5k.

findings.headline: Debt write-offs made without independent authorization, contrary to council policy
findings.detail: In June 2025, two debts under £2k were both raised and authorized by the same Senior Finance Officer without the required independent review. The CIVICA finance system does not enforce segregation of duties. A review confirmed this did not occur elsewhere that year, but the control gap allowed it once.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties in debt decisions is a core financial control. Failure means one officer can write off council money without scrutiny, risking loss or error.
findings.figures: Two debts under £2k (June 2025)
findings.quote: In June 2025, two debts under £2k were both raised, and authorised for write-off, by the Senior Finance Officer without independent review.

findings.headline: Quality assurance programme incomplete with self-assessment deferred and external assessment deep-dive not carried out for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has not completed its 2025/26 internal self-assessment as it is waiting to present results of a gap analysis against new Global Internal Audit Standards in the UK Public Sector later this year. Additionally, the external quality assessment deep-dive review of audit files has not been completed for 2025/26 audits. The last external quality assessment (October 2022) resulted in 'generally conforms' with 60 out of 64 areas conforming, but two areas of partial conformance remain unresolved regarding assurance mapping and timely five-year reassessment scheduling.
findings.matters: Incomplete quality assurance processes mean there is no current independent validation that internal audit standards are being met, reducing external assurance on the reliability of audit opinions.
findings.figures: Self-assessment deferred to later in 2026; external deep-dive review not completed; last EQA October 2022
findings.quote: A self-assessment has not been completed for 2025/26. This is because a gap analysis was completed against the new GIAS in the UK Public Sector, the results of which will be presented to the Committee later this year. PSIAS compliance - deep dive review of files - 100%. Four files per quarter N/A Not completed on 2025/26 audits

findings.headline: Internal audit contractor performance is below contract standards with quality payment withheld and contract being re-procured
findings.detail: Performance against key performance indicators shows only 5 out of 10 metrics fully met, 4 partially met, and 1 not met. Specific failures include draft reports not issued within 10 working days of fieldwork in 1 of 4 quarters, final reports not issued within 5 working days in 1 of 4 quarters, and quarterly performance packs not reported on time. As a result, the 10% quality payment withheld until year-end was adjusted and not paid in full. The contract is now being re-procured for the 2027/28 audit year.
findings.matters: Audit contractor underperformance reduces confidence in the quality and timeliness of control assessments; contract re-procurement suggests the council recognises the incumbent provider is not meeting delivery standards.
findings.figures: 5 KPIs fully met, 4 partially met, 1 not met; quality payment reduced; contract re-procurement scheduled
findings.quote: The overall performance status is determined as 'Amber' with only five 'fully met', four 'partially met' and one 'not met'. As the Contractor does not have exclusivity, BDO LLP and the shared internal audit service at Hertfordshire County Council continue to be used on half of the Consortium's Internal Audit Plan as well as EIAS auditors. The contract is now being re-procured ready to be in place for the 2027/28 audit year.

findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit gives qualified reasonable assurance due to persistent control weaknesses, particularly in high-risk areas including contract management and Section 106 agreements
findings.detail: The opinion is 'reasonable' rather than 'substantial', qualified by identified weaknesses in risk management, governance, and internal controls. Internal controls are found to be ineffective in Environmental Health - Licensing. Risk management arrangements show prolonged delays in implementing agreed actions and continued exposure in high-risk areas including licensing income, Section 106 agreements, private sector housing, and contract management. Control weaknesses leave the council exposed to financial loss, regulatory breach, and reduced service effectiveness.
findings.matters: Qualified reasonable assurance (rather than substantial) signals to lenders that internal controls have identified gaps in governance and risk mitigation that may affect the council's ability to safeguard assets and manage financial risk.
findings.figures: Reasonable (not Substantial) opinion; 1 Limited audit (2025/26), 5 Reasonable audits; 2 high-risk areas carried over with unresolved risks from prior years
findings.quote: There are weaknesses in the Council's internal control, risk management, and governance arrangements. The persistence of overdue recommendations, including urgent actions, alongside areas of statutory non-compliance and ineffective control processes, reduces assurance that risks are being managed effectively. The Council remains exposed to risks of financial loss, regulatory breach, and reduced service effectiveness.

findings.headline: Audit recommendations overdue are increasing and include items from 2021/22 still awaiting implementation
findings.detail: 23 recommendations were past their due date at year-end (up from 19 in 2024/25), including 2 urgent and 18 important. Notably, one important recommendation on Key Controls and Assurance relating to penalty charge notice income dating from 2021/22 remains outstanding with a revised due date of June 2026 — nearly four years past the original deadline. Eight recommendations from the 2024/25 Section 106 Arrangements limited audit remain overdue with revised dates to July 2026, affecting the council's ability to manage s106 agreements and funds.
findings.matters: Growing backlogs of overdue audit recommendations indicate governance arrangements are not ensuring accountability and timely delivery of control improvements, reducing confidence that identified risks are being actively mitigated.
findings.figures: 23 overdue recommendations (2 urgent, 18 important, 3 routine) vs 19 in 2024/25. One from 2021/22, eight from 2024/25 Section 106 audit.
findings.quote: the position at year end, as shown in the table below, is that 23 recommendations (2024/25 – 19) were past their due at year-end, two of which were urgent. One important recommendation remains past its due date from 2021/22 - Key Controls and Assurance relating to the income from penalty charge notices; this now has a revised due date of June 2026. I note that eight recommendations (one urgent, six important and one routine) out of the ten made in the 'Limited' Section 106 Arrangements 2024/25 audit remain past their due dates and are in progress, with revised due dates up to July 2026.

findings.headline: Licensing income collection does not meet statutory requirements and weaknesses remain past correction deadline
findings.detail: The Environmental Health - Licensing audit found weaknesses in monitoring annual fees for premises licences, with no automated invoicing or reconciliation tracking. The Licensing Act 2003 requires suspension of a license where payment is not received, but the council is non-compliant with this obligation. An urgent recommendation to automate invoicing was closed post year-end, but an important recommendation requiring alignment with statutory requirements remains overdue with revised deadline June 2026.
findings.matters: Income collection is a basic control, and non-compliance with mandatory statutory suspension requirements exposes the council to legal challenge and creates an enforcement gap in licensing management.
findings.figures: 1 urgent recommendation (closed post year-end), 1 important recommendation (overdue, revised due June 2026)
findings.quote: To integrate automated invoicing functionality to enable annual licence fees to be promptly billed and collected and introduce a reconciliation and tracking process to identify unpaid licences and recover outstanding fees to ensure that debtors are identified in a timely manner and dealt with in accordance with the Licensing Act 2003. (Urgent) This recommendation was closed post year-end. Review the Council's Licensing Policy to ensure it aligns with section 55A of the Licensing Act 2003, suspend a premises licence if the holder has failed to pay the annual fee, and invoke the legislative requirement to suspend licenses where payment has been requested but not received. (Important) This recommendation is past its due date and has a revised due date of June 2026.

findings.headline: Renters Rights Act 2025 creating new statutory implementation workload with service-wide impact
findings.detail: The Renters' Rights Act 2025 introduces new statutory requirements affecting multiple council service areas. The risk (residual score 12) is flagged as generating additional workload through implementation requirements and landlord actions ahead of the legislation taking effect. The council reports that tranche one delivery is complete with required policy adopted at committee; background processes are developed ready for 1 May 2026 enactment date.
findings.matters: New statutory obligations often create cost and service pressures that were not budgeted. This is happening alongside LGR and food waste implementation — a three-front workload expansion with no clear funding source.
findings.figures: Risk score 4x3=12 residual; 1 May 2026 enactment date; tranche one implementation complete
findings.quote: The required policy has been completed and is on the next committee agenda for adoption. The background processes are developed ready for the 1st May enactment date.

findings.headline: Cyber security leadership gap: key postholder promoted without replacement, reducing oversight during LGR transition
findings.detail: The officer responsible for cyber security oversight has been promoted to other priorities and the post has not been backfilled. Risk score remains 9 (was 9) but the register explicitly flags this as a concern. Phishing testing shows improvement (13% click rate vs 30% previously), but capacity for cyber governance and testing has been reduced during a period when LGR workstreams are already adding pressure.
findings.matters: A lender monitoring operational risk needs to know whether the council has adequate oversight of its digital security during a high-pressure organisational transition. Key person dependency in cyber governance is a material governance weakness.
findings.figures: Cyber risk score 3x3=9 residual; phishing click rate improved to 13% from 30%
findings.quote: The Cyber risk is increased as the postholder who was overseeing Cyber Security now has been promoted and has additional priorities and the post hasn't been back filled.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating organisational capacity pressures alongside food waste implementation and Renters Rights Act rollout
findings.detail: North Norfolk is one of 8 councils preparing to merge into 3 new unitary authorities by April 2028. The mayoral devolution election scheduled for May 2026 has been postponed to May 2028. Residual risk score is 8 (was 12) but the council notes that "capacity issues generated by Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation" are straining teams already managing food waste implementation and Renters Rights Act statutory requirements. Work is proceeding collaboratively across all seven district councils.
findings.matters: LGR creates both opportunity and risk for lenders. Organisational churn during merger preparation can slow service delivery and drain management attention from financial discipline. The overlap with multiple new statutory obligations is a compounding pressure.
findings.figures: 3 new unitary councils to be formed by April 2028; mayoral election postponed from May 2026 to May 2028; residual risk score 8 (down from 12)
findings.quote: Whether there is sufficient capacity to address the work that will be involved in preparing for LGR including the necessary governance, the structures and finance alongside other emerging issues e.g. the implementation of a separate food waste collection by March 2026.

findings.headline: Mandatory domestic food waste collection service launch delayed to early 2027, missing statutory April 2026 deadline due to national vehicle supply shortage
findings.detail: The council's statutory obligation to introduce weekly domestic food waste collections (part of amended Environment Act 2021) has slipped from April 2026 to early 2027. Risk score reduced from 12 to 9 as depot lease issues are being resolved and benchmarking commissioned to validate Serco contractor costs. The delay is attributed to high national demand exceeding vehicle supplier capacity, which affects all councils.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know when mandatory service costs will hit the budget. A national delay signals that other councils face the same pressure; costs are likely to be higher than budgeted if suppliers are constrained.
findings.figures: Residual risk score reduced from 12 to 9; go-live date now early 2027 (was April 2026); delays attributed to national vehicle supply shortage
findings.quote: Delays to the delivery of collection vehicles have resulted in a delay to the go-live date for service introduction into early 2027 but this is felt nationally due to the high demand not being able to be met by suppliers.

findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan remains red with residual score 16 despite balanced budget, due to uncertainty about costs of new statutory requirements and Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council set a balanced 2025/26 budget with forecast surplus, but faces unresolved cost pressures from mandatory domestic food waste collections and Renters Rights Act implementation. Local Government Reorganisation is also creating planning uncertainty. The risk score is unchanged at 16 and will not be reassessed until an updated Medium Term Financial Strategy is presented in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to know when the council will have visibility on its medium-term sustainability. This red risk flags that the council does not yet know what future service costs will actually be.
findings.figures: Balanced budget set February 2026; forecast surplus at period 10 monitoring; outturn results scheduled July 2026
findings.quote: Whilst the narrative demonstrates progress has been made following the settlement in December 2025, setting of a balanced budget and forecast surplus in the 2025/2026 budget outturn, there remains uncertainty relating to global economics, upcoming expenditure relating to new statutory requirements (domestic food waste collections and Renters Rights Act implementation) alongside the preparation and progression of Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Report GRAC Q4
findings.headline: The council explicitly acknowledges heightened risk to delivery capacity from the new Local Plan requirement and warns of potential legal, operational and reputational consequences of failure.
findings.detail: In recommending CR 046 be added to the corporate register, the council states there is a heightened risk relating to capacity, resources, programme delivery and compliance. It warns that failure to meet requirements could have substantial legal, operational and reputational implications, and notes the development plan underpins all planning decisions.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council has the management capacity and stability to sustain core functions; this signals the council recognises its own resource constraints in delivering a statutory obligation.
findings.figures: 30-month delivery window (complexity of plan-making, extended duration of previous process)
findings.quote: Given the complexity of plan-making and the extended duration of the previous Local Plan process, there is a heightened risk relating to capacity, resources, programme delivery, and compliance with evolving national requirements.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Report GRAC Q4
findings.headline: Government has set a 30-month deadline to review and prepare a new Local Plan, which the council describes as extremely tight and creates heightened delivery risk.
findings.detail: Following Local Plan adoption in December 2025, government introduced a statutory requirement for councils to prepare a new-style Local Plan under updated legislation (PCPA 2004 as amended by LURA 2023). The council explicitly identifies the 30-month deadline as an extremely tight timescale given how long the recently adopted plan took to complete. The council is formally adding this as corporate risk CR 046, flagging heightened risk relating to capacity, resources, programme delivery, and compliance with evolving national requirements.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver a statutory development plan on time could result in substantial legal, operational, and reputational consequences that affect the council's core planning function and credibility.
findings.figures: 30 months (government-mandated deadline)
findings.quote: The timescale to complete the review in accordance with legislative requirements is set by Government as 30 months. This is an extremely tight timescale given the length of time that the recently adopted plan took to complete.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales collapse 79%, from £2.95m to £0.6m
findings.detail: Capital receipts available to fund future capital projects drop from £2.953m (2025/26 budget) to £0.625m (2026/27 budget), a 79% reduction. This severely constrains the council's ability to recycle proceeds from asset disposals back into new capital investment.
findings.matters: Signals fewer asset disposals or lower proceeds from sales, limiting financial flexibility and reinvestment capacity. Compounds the capital programme retrenchment already driven by grant funding loss.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision costs acknowledged as escalating long-term risk under chosen accounting method
findings.detail: The council uses the Asset Life Basis (annuity) method for MRP, which the strategy explicitly identifies carries a forward risk: MRP costs will escalate over time. The proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream rises from 2.61% (2025/26) to 2.98% (2027/28), consuming an increasing share of the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Growing debt servicing costs will consume an increasing share of the revenue budget over the medium term, limiting flexibility for services and creating future affordability pressure. The council is aware of this risk but chose the accounting method anyway.
findings.quote: The risk of this method is that MRP costs will escalate over time, leading to higher MRP costs in the long-term

findings.headline: Council relies on commercial property portfolio to reduce budget deficits and support revenue
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states that the council's commercial property holdings are held primarily to generate income supporting the operational revenue budget. Section 7 discusses using property investments to help 'reducing Council budget deficits' and managing a portfolio 'to support the delivery of services'.
findings.matters: Indicates structural revenue budget pressure — the council is dependent on volatile commercial property income to help balance operational budgets rather than demonstrating sustainable revenue-funded services. Property income carries concentration risk and is cyclical.
findings.figures: None specified; portfolio described as 'small' but expanding
findings.quote: Land and property assets can play a key role in reducing Council budget deficits and generating both capital and revenue income

findings.headline: Government capital grant funding falls 63%, from £24.5m to £9.1m
findings.detail: Capital grants collapse from £24.523m (2025/26 budget) to £9.148m (2026/27 budget). This is the largest single financing source for the capital programme and its near-halving is the primary driver of the overall capital programme contraction. No explanation is provided for the loss of external funding.
findings.matters: Indicates loss of external capital funding from government, suggesting either reduced government support priority or the council has lower competitive standing for grants. This reduces financial flexibility and forces reliance on internal reserves or reduced capital ambition.

findings.headline: Approved capital programme collapses 64% year-on-year, from £38.3m to £9.5m
findings.detail: The council's approved capital programme drops from £38.328m (2025/26 budget) to £9.461m (2026/27 budget). Even with capital bids under review (£4.480m additional), total planned capital expenditure is 64% below the prior year. This follows actual 2024/25 spend of £25.7m, suggesting a fundamental retrenchment in capital ambitions.
findings.matters: Signals either completion of major capital projects or constrained capital spending capacity. For a lender, indicates reduced investment in council assets and potentially weaker growth prospects for the authority.
findings.quote: Approved Capital Programme 25.702 38.328 9.461 2.300 2.000

findings.headline: Car park income (13% of revenue) is demand-led and price-sensitive; fee increases planned for April 2026
findings.detail: The council generates £3.1m in car park income, which is identified as 'regularly monitored' due to external and seasonal factors. Council is raising car park fees on 7 April 2026. Income assumptions remain subject to economic uncertainty and demand risk.
findings.matters: Material income source is vulnerable to recession or behaviour change. Council is increasing prices during uncertain economic period, which could trigger demand-led shortfall.
findings.figures: Car park income budget: £3.1m. Represents 13% of 2026/27 budgeted income. Fee rise implemented April 2026.
findings.quote: This area generates a significant level of income for the Council which in turn supports the delivery of other services across the Council. As this is a demand led service which is influenced by external factors this area is regularly monitored. The 2025/26 budget currently assumes gross income of over £3.1m from all car parking related fees and charges.

findings.headline: Council is using reserve drawdowns to balance budget; General Fund reserve will not sustain multi-year deficits
findings.detail: The 2026/27 balanced budget requires £788k contribution to earmarked reserves to offset a £1m underlying surplus that masks funding redistribution. The General Fund reserve, forecast at £2.9m at end 2026/27, is only £0.8m above the s151 officer's minimum prudent level of £2.1m. At current trajectory of reserve usage for LGR, net zero, and housing costs, reserves will deplete.
findings.matters: Council is not balancing budget through sustainable operational decisions; it is drawing reserves. Reserves are finite and the council acknowledges it has 'fragile' funding environment.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve (2025/26): £2.6m forecast. After 2026/27 allocation: £2.9m. Minimum prudent level: £2.1m. Earmarked reserves: £13.4m at end 2025/26.
findings.quote: Line 26, Column D shows the net surplus being allocated to earmarked reserves, i.e. £0.788m.

findings.headline: Funding 'cliff edge' risk after 2028/29 when transitional protections expire; settlement does not address long-term adequacy
findings.detail: The three-year settlement (to 2028/29) relies heavily on transitional protections and funding floors to prevent immediate cash reductions. These protections will unwind beyond 2028/29, creating an unquantified risk of a sharp funding drop. Government settlement 'does not address underlying funding adequacy'.
findings.matters: Even if council balances budget to 2028/29, faces potential material drop in available funding when government props are withdrawn. Creates existential risk beyond current plan horizon.
findings.figures: Three-year settlement period 2026/27–2028/29. Cliff edge timing and magnitude unknown.
findings.quote: it does not address underlying funding adequacy and creates ongoing risks beyond 2028/29, particularly due to the scale of transitional protections and the potential for a funding 'cliff edge' when these unwind.

findings.headline: Unfunded new burdens (food waste collection, LGR responsibilities) are creating cost pressure with no matching government funding
findings.detail: Government has mandated separate domestic food waste collection and imposed LGR costs on councils 'with insufficient funding'. These are adding pressure to 'already constrained revenue budgets' but the specific financial exposure is embedded in line budgets rather than quantified separately.
findings.matters: Council has mandated costs it did not plan for and cannot avoid. Reduces financial flexibility and risks overspends if commercial negotiations on waste contract cost more than forecast.
findings.figures: Not separately quantified; costs incorporated into service budgets and noted as part of budget pressure context.
findings.quote: new burdens have been placed on the Council with insufficient funding including Local Government Reorganisation and a domestic food waste collection service

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs are unquantified but substantial; council may cease to exist after 2027/28
findings.detail: Council has created a £750k reserve to cover LGR costs, but the government has not specified what those costs will be. The cabinet decision on Norfolk's reorganisation is expected March 2026. Council notes it 'would cease to exist after the 2027/2028 financial year' under current understanding. Actual costs to be determined.
findings.matters: Material financial liability with timing and amount unknown. If LGR costs exceed the £750k reserve, council will face unbudgeted pressure or further reserve drawdowns. Uncertainty over council's post-2028 existence complicates longer-term borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: £750k earmarked reserve created for LGR. Cabinet decision on Norfolk expected March 2026.
findings.quote: Government has indicated the cost of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is to be borne by the affected Councils including NNDC. The precise costs are yet to be determined and will be driven in part by the 'minded to' decision for Norfolk expected in March 2026.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan projects unmet deficits of £0.6m–£1.1m in 2027–29 requiring substantial cost reductions
findings.detail: After using earmarked reserves to balance the budget, the MTFS shows unmet deficits of £582k (2027/28) and £1.109m (2028/29). The document states 'substantial work will have to be undertaken' to reach a balanced position. Current balance in 2026/27 masks the underlying deterioration.
findings.matters: Council cannot sustain service levels at current spending. Lender needs visibility on what cost reductions or further reserve drawdowns are planned.
findings.figures: 2027/28 unmet deficit: £0.582m. 2028/29 unmet deficit: £1.109m (per Table 13: Projected Deficit over life of MTFS).
findings.quote: Looking beyond 2026/27, the financial projections included in the MTFS indicate that substantial work will have to be undertaken in order to reach a balanced budget position.

findings.headline: Government funding per head is declining 23% while English average rises 24%, leaving this council structurally weaker than peers
findings.detail: North Norfolk will see funding per capita fall from £105.38 (2024/25) to £80.99 (2028/29), while the national average increases. The council is reliant on a 95% government funding floor to avoid real-terms cash reductions. This is explicitly identified as reinforcing 'structural weakness of district council funding' within the reformed system.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's financial position is stable or declining in structural terms. This shows deliberate government policy choice redistributing funding away from district councils, not a temporary fluctuation.
findings.figures: Government funding per head 2024/25: £105.38; 2028/29: £80.99 (23% fall). District councils receiving 3.3% Core Spending Power growth over 3 years vs 15% national average.
findings.quote: Government funding per head of population is projected to decrease by 23% from 2024/25 (£105.38 per head) to 2028/29 (£80.99 per head). In comparison English authorities overall will increase by 24%.

findings.headline: Council tax now critical to funding gap closure; maximum annual increases planned indefinitely
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes NNDC will increase its precept annually by the maximum allowed (3% or £5, whichever is greater). The document states that government funding calculations assume councils will apply maximum increases, meaning the settlement is not guaranteed unless this assumption is delivered. This creates a dependency on council tax for financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Reliance on council tax increases to close structural deficits is politically constrained and signals inability to manage within baseline funding. If increases are not delivered (due to political pressure or referendum risk if threshold is crossed), the council faces immediate further budget pressure.
findings.figures: Current Band D charge retained by NNDC: £173.52; subject to 3% or £5 cap whichever is greater
findings.quote: Central government funding calculations for local authorities are based on the assumption that councils will apply the maximum permitted increase in council tax for the relevant year. Where a lower increase is applied, this creates a corresponding shortfall against the funding assumptions built into the national settlement.

findings.headline: Reserve position excludes anticipated deficits; actual reserves may be lower than projected
findings.detail: Chart 7 projects reserves rising from £16.5m (April 2025) to £17.2m (April 2028). However, the document explicitly states these projections 'do not take into account the anticipated deficit positions for future years, or potential usage of reserves in future years budgeting for reasons not yet known to the authority.' This means actual reserves could be substantially lower if deficits are funded from reserves.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's financial buffer for unexpected costs and misforecasts. If deficits of £1.5-2m are funded from reserves annually, the council's reserves could fall to £12-13m within three years, reducing financial resilience and ability to respond to shocks.
findings.figures: Projected reserves April 2025: £16.5m; April 2028: £17.2m (before deficit impact)
findings.quote: Please note that these movements do not take into account the anticipated deficit positions for future years, or potential usage of reserves in future years budgeting for reasons not yet known to the authority.

findings.headline: New statutory duty (domestic food waste collection) with uncertain and potentially inadequate funding
findings.detail: The council faces a new statutory burden to implement separate domestic food waste collection from residents. New burdens funding is being rolled into core settlement funding with no separate identification. The council states it cannot yet confirm robust costings, meaning the true cost of this mandate is unknown and could exceed allocated funding, creating a hidden pressure on the budget.
findings.matters: Unfunded or underfunded statutory duties are impossible to decline and create a ratchet effect on the budget. If funding proves inadequate, the council must either cut other services or draw reserves.
findings.figures: Not separately quantified in the settlement; funding rolled into core allocation
findings.quote: At this stage, there remains uncertainty around the most appropriate service delivery model for NNDC. As a result, robust costings cannot yet be confirmed, and assumptions have been built within the MTFS based latest information available at the time of writing.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates strategic and financial uncertainty until at least March 2026 decision
findings.detail: The council faces a period where it cannot commit to long-term structural changes or recurring expenditure while its future governance framework is unresolved. A 'minded-to' decision is expected in March 2026, with vesting day anticipated for April 2028. The council explicitly states this uncertainty constrains its ability to progress detailed joint financial planning or structural efficiency work that might otherwise close the budget gap.
findings.matters: Inability to plan structural efficiencies or partnerships creates a two-year window where the council must manage deficits without pursuing the most material cost reductions, increasing reserve drawdown risk and limiting financial options.
findings.figures: Minded-to decision expected March 2026; implementation vesting date anticipated 1 April 2028
findings.quote: For North Norfolk District Council, the LGR process introduces a period of strategic and financial uncertainty which must be reflected within the MTFS. In particular, the Council must consider the risk of committing to recurring expenditure, long-term savings plans, or significant structural change while the future governance framework remains unresolved.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review and Business Rates Reset remove £3.2m of historic income annually from 2026/27
findings.detail: Business rates reset incorporates historic growth into baseline funding, removing accumulated growth previously retained locally. NNDC loses the New Homes Bonus (which it received) from April 2026. The Fair Funding Review reduces district council funding relative to upper-tier authorities. These changes create a structural step-change in the council's funding base rather than a gradual pressure.
findings.matters: A permanent reduction in baseline funding changes the council's structural financial position. Unlike a temporary grant cut, this is embedded in the new funding system and reduces the council's financial flexibility and debt service capacity.
findings.figures: Business Rates income: £8.999m (2025/26) to £5.425m (2026/27); New Homes Bonus abolished entirely from April 2026
findings.quote: For North Norfolk District Council, settlement funding in prior years comprised several elements... From 2026/27 onwards, many of these funding streams are either abolished or rolled into a single core settlement, reducing transparency and flexibility within the funding system.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficits growing from £935k to £1.96m across the MTFS period
findings.detail: The council projects deficits of £935,365 in 2027/28, rising to £1,521,330 in 2028/29 and £1,963,744 in 2029/30. These are not one-off pressures but reflect a structural mismatch between costs and funding. The document notes these deficits are not accounted for in the current reserve projections.
findings.matters: Growing deficits that are structural rather than cyclical signal the council cannot sustain current service levels without intervention, creating refinancing risk and pressure on reserves.
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting a deficit position for the coming years.

findings.headline: Project Management Framework in place for over two years but not universally adopted across the council
findings.detail: A Project Management Framework has existed for over two years but is not being adopted universally across the organisation. The council acknowledges this represents a weakness in governance and work will be undertaken to enforce its use.
findings.matters: If project governance is not consistently applied, capital projects and strategic initiatives may slip cost or schedule controls, affecting the council's ability to manage borrowing and project delivery.
findings.figures: Framework in place 2+ years; adoption level not specified
findings.quote: Whilst this has been in place for over two years the framework is not being adopted universally across the council and so at present this does represent a weakness in governance

findings.headline: Waste Management (commercial and garden) audit found 2 urgent and 5 important breaches requiring remediation
findings.detail: Waste Management audit (commercial and garden waste services) was rated limited assurance with two urgent action points, five important actions, and one routine action. System documentation notes to be completed following implementation of a new commercial customer database, with completion target 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: Waste services are often a revenue-generating or cost-centre activity; urgent control failures suggest either financial mismanagement or service delivery failure affecting income or expenditure.
findings.figures: 2 urgent, 5 important, 1 routine action points; completion 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Waste Management – Commercial and garden waste where there were 2 urgent, 5 important, 1 routine action points to address

findings.headline: Section 106 developer contributions audit found 1 urgent, 8 important, and 1 routine breach requiring remediation
findings.detail: Section 106 Arrangements audit (developer contributions held on behalf of services) was rated limited assurance with one urgent action point, eight important actions, and one routine action. The council has committed to implement urgent recommendations ASAP and important ones within 3 months, with completion by July 2026, following appointment of a new Section 106 officer after a service delivery gap.
findings.matters: Section 106 funds are developer obligations often held in trust; control failures here indicate either improper use of restricted monies or loss/misapplication of funds a lender is entitled to assume the council retains.
findings.figures: 1 urgent, 8 important, 1 routine action points; completion target July 2026
findings.quote: Section 106 Arrangements where there were 1 urgent, 8 important, and 1 routine action points to address

findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit gave split 'reasonable/limited assurance' opinion, reflecting material concerns about the control environment
findings.detail: The HIA's annual opinion is described as 'concerning'. Five completed audits received limited assurance: Section 106 Arrangements, Private Sector Housing (HMOs/empty homes), Risk Management, Environmental Charter, and Waste Management. This split opinion reflects 'potential direction of travel in the control environment'. The council has 19 outstanding audit recommendations at year-end (down from 41 prior year).
findings.matters: A split or limited assurance opinion on governance and internal controls indicates material weaknesses; the direction-of-travel language suggests deterioration in the control environment despite some recommendation closures.
findings.figures: 5 audits with limited assurance out of 15 completed; 19 outstanding recommendations vs. 41 prior year
findings.quote: A reasonable/limited audit opinion was given for the year overall in relation to the framework of Governance, Risk Management and Control. This opinion is consistent with the opinion given for the previous year. The split opinion given by the HIA reflects the potential direction of travel in the control environment at the Council

findings.headline: Prior years' Statements of Accounts issued with disclaimed audit opinions and 2024/25 identified further financial reporting control weaknesses
findings.detail: The council's Statements of Accounts for 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24 all received disclaimed audit opinions from external auditors. In the 2024/25 audit, external auditors identified areas where financial reporting processes and supporting controls require strengthening, including gaps in capacity, documentation clarity, and review arrangements. The council has agreed a management action plan with implementation monitored through GRAC.
findings.matters: A lender cannot trust a council's financial position if prior accounts are disclaimed or current-year controls are weak; without reliable accounts, assessing debt serviceability and financial sustainability becomes impossible.
findings.figures: 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 — disclaimed; 2024/25 — identified control gaps requiring remediation
findings.quote: the 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24 Statements of Accounts were issued with disclaimed audit opinions. During the 2024/25 audit, the external auditor identified areas where the Council's financial reporting processes and supporting controls could be strengthened to improve the quality, consistency and timeliness of the Statement of Accounts

findings.headline: Large portions of the audit remain incomplete and may influence the final opinion
findings.detail: As of the report date, the auditors have been unable to complete work on multiple significant areas: Balance Sheet items (Short-Term Debtors, Creditors, Provisions, PPE Valuations, IFRS 16 Leases, Reserves, Capital Grants); Income and Expenditure Statement areas; Cash Flow; GL System Change; and Whole of Government Accounts. The report states: "Given that the audit process is still ongoing, we will continue to challenge the remaining evidence provided and the final disclosures in the Statement of Accounts which could influence our final audit opinion."
findings.matters: Incomplete audit work means there is a continuing risk of further misstatements being identified. The final opinion has not yet been issued and could worsen. This adds uncertainty to the council's financial reporting.
findings.figures: Audit commenced: 17 November 2025. Backstop date for opinion: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Given that the audit process is still ongoing, we will continue to challenge the remaining evidence provided and the final disclosures in the Statement of Accounts which could influence our final audit opinion.

findings.headline: There is no formalised procedure for review and approval of journal entries before posting to the general ledger
findings.detail: The auditors identified a control observation that the Council has no formalised procedure for reviewing and approving journal entries before they are posted to the general ledger. This is a material internal control gap. The auditors noted they have not yet completed journals testing, so they have not concluded whether any improper entries exist.
